overview: Visual counting measures how accurately you can scan a busy image and keep track of one kind of shape among several. In IQ tests this appears as timed counting tasks, where a systematic scan matters more than a quick glance.

strategy.b: Always scan the grid in the same pattern: left to right along each row, then down to the next row. A fixed route means you cover every cell once and never double count.
Recognise groups of one to four at a glance rather than counting each shape one by one. Grouping shapes into pairs keeps the count quick and reliable.
Keep a running count for each row, and only add the rows together at the end. Several small counts are easier to check than one large count made in a single pass.
Once you have a count, scan the grid a second time in a different direction, such as column by column. If both totals match, your answer is almost certainly right.

fig.title: Scan each row in order
fig.note: Triangles per row: 2, 2 and 1, so the total is 5.

drills.name: Count triangles
drills.how: Scan the grid row by row and count only triangles, ignoring every other shape even when it looks similar. Keep a separate count for each row so you can check each row on its own.
drills.tip: Name the target silently each time you spot one, which keeps your attention locked on that shape alone.
drills.mistake: Counting a shape twice when it sits at the end of one row and the start of the next. Fix it by finishing each row fully before you move to the next, and never looking back.

ex.q: A grid has three rows. Row 1: triangle, circle, triangle, square. Row 2: star, triangle, circle, triangle. Row 3: square, circle, triangle, star. How many triangles are there?
ex.why: Count each row separately: row 1 has 2 triangles, row 2 has 2 and row 3 has 1, giving 5 in total.

drills.name: Count circles
drills.how: Circles are easy to confuse with rounded shapes in a dense grid, so check that each one has smooth, unbroken curves before adding it. Go row by row and keep a running total for each row.
drills.tip: Group circles in pairs as you go, so you can add them quickly instead of counting one at a time.
drills.mistake: Counting a shape that is only partly visible or overlapped. Fix it by counting only complete shapes and noting any unclear one to recheck on your second scan.

ex.q: Row 1: circle, square, circle, circle. Row 2: triangle, circle, star, square. Row 3: circle, diamond, square, circle. How many circles are there?
ex.why: Row 1 has three circles, row 2 has one and row 3 has two, so the total is six.

drills.name: Count squares
drills.how: Squares are easy to mix up with diamonds, so check each shape's edges: a square sits flat with level sides, while a diamond is tilted onto a point. Work row by row and keep a count for each row before adding them up.
drills.tip: Scan for flat, level edges first and ignore anything tilted onto a point.
drills.mistake: Including a diamond because it also has four sides. Fix it by checking whether the sides are level, since a tilted shape is a diamond, not a square.

ex.q: Row 1: square, star, triangle, square. Row 2: circle, square, square, diamond. Row 3: star, triangle, circle, square. How many squares are there?
ex.why: Row 1 has two squares, row 2 has two and row 3 has one, giving five. The diamond and the stars are not squares, so they are excluded.

drills.name: Count diamonds
drills.how: Diamonds are squares tilted onto a point, with sharp points at the top, bottom, left and right, so they can be missed when they are small. Scan each row for those sharp points, and tally diamonds separately from every other shape.
drills.tip: Look for the four sharp points rather than the overall outline of the shape.
drills.mistake: Counting squares as diamonds, or the reverse, when the shapes are small. Fix it by checking each shape's points against its flat sides before you add it to the tally.

ex.q: Row 1: diamond, star, diamond, circle. Row 2: square, diamond, triangle, triangle. Row 3: circle, star, diamond, square. How many diamonds are there?
ex.why: Row 1 has two diamonds, row 2 has one and row 3 has one, so the total is four.

drills.name: Count stars
drills.how: Stars have several spiky points, so check how many points each shape has before you tally it. Scan row by row, and keep the star total separate from any other shape you notice.
drills.tip: Most stars have five points, so a shape with fewer spikes is not a star.
drills.mistake: Missing stars at the edges of a row because your eyes drift toward the centre. Fix it by reading each row from its left edge to its right edge, in order.

ex.q: Row 1: star, triangle, star, square. Row 2: diamond, star, circle, star. Row 3: triangle, square, star, circle. How many stars are there?
ex.why: Row 1 has two stars, row 2 has two and row 3 has one, so the total is five.

levels: Level 1: count one target shape in a small grid of two rows and four columns.
Level 2: count one target shape in a three by four grid with clear spacing between shapes.
Level 3: count one target among four or more shape types in a three by five grid.
Level 4: count a target shape in a larger grid where some shapes are rotated or slightly smaller.
Level 5: count two target shapes in one scan, keeping separate totals under time pressure.
Level 6: count a target in a dense grid of similar shapes, then confirm the total with a second scan.
routine: Day 1: do 3 small grid counts row by row, saying each row's total aloud.
Day 2: practise subitising by looking at a group of 1 to 4 shapes for two seconds and naming the number without counting one by one.
Day 3: count one target shape in 5 grids, then check each answer with a column scan.
Day 4: time yourself on 10 mixed count items, aiming for about 15 seconds each.
Day 5: review every missed item and note whether the cause was a skipped cell or a confused shape.
